title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false match in an automated licence-plate recognition system, occurring at the point where a camera reading is passed to officers as an enforcement lead. The system compared a misread plate against a stolen-vehicle record and produced a hit on a car that was not the stolen one. The failure sits in the identification step, before any human contact, and it escalated into an armed stop.

Catching it would have required verification of the alert against the plate itself before officers approached. The reporting states that the sheriff's office attributed the misread to an illegal tinted plate cover and called the deputy's actions reasonable, while Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement. That places the disputed question at the handoff between the system's output and the officer's decision to act on it.

What is not established is whether the plate cover actually caused the misread, whether the deputy had time or means to verify before drawing a weapon, and whether any policy required verification at that moment. The account of the incident rests on a single outlet's reporting, and the characterisations by the sheriff's office and by Flock are statements by the parties, not findings.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, a 42-year-old motorist in York County, South Carolina, was reportedly held at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction and called the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
title_en: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover
